Cromolitografie imprimată pe hârtie tipografică lucioasă, în format carte poștală. Prezintă o imagine cu piscina publică din Erie, Pennsylvania, Statele Unite ale Americii. În partea de sus a imaginii, text realizat prin tipărire: „Public Swimming Pool, / Erie, Pa.” Verso: rubricatură de carte poștală, cu spații dedicate scrierii mesajului („The space for writing messages” - text imprimat cu tuș albastru) și adresei („This space for address” - text imprimat cu tuș albastru); ștampila poștală a localității Erie, Pa, cu data de 14 noiembrie 1910; timbrul a fost desprins, probabil pentru a se verifica dacă există un mesaj secret, practică des întâlnită pentru cărțile poștale ale începutului de secol al XX lea. Destinatarul acestei cărți poștale este: „Mr. Ilie Martin / comerciant / Szelistye / (...) / Hungary / Europa”. Însemnare manuscrisă, greu descifrabilă, în limba engleză: „Erie, Pa. 13/XI.910 / Dear ... / You must not laugh at this / letter. I am writing English / for the first timne. I have / been here in America / now about nine weeks. / The city were I lives is / called Erie, Pa. After three / days I found work. I / like to live in America. / Yout truly / Olimpiu / short st. 212.” (Dragă ... / Nu trebuie să râzi de această / scrisoare. Scriu engleză / pentru prima dată. Am / ajuns aici în America / acum vreo nouă săptămâni. / Orașul în care trăiesc se numește Erie, Pa. După trei zile am găsit de lucru. Îmi place să trăiesc în America. / Al tău / Olimpiu). În partea stângă, cu tuș albastru, imprimat textul: „Published exclusively for S.H. KNOX and Co / Made in U.S.A.”. Număr de inventar: MCPT 2636.

I B 57"), însemnare manuscrisă cu stiloul "Fete și feciori din Glogon. Comint. Timiș-Torantal / Foto ing. Th. Filipescu, 15 august 1903", ștampilă "Muzeul "Brukenthal" Sibiu / Nr. 14.304" (cifră scrisă cu cerneală și tăiată); număr inventar MCPR 510.

Fotografie de exterior, realizată pe uilța unui sat. Imaginea este realizată prin reproducere tipografică prin imprimare. Prezintă evacuarea satului Lukova, Albania, din calea polonezilor, în 20 iunie 1915. În centrul imaginii se remarcă două femei, una dintre ele ținând un copil mic în brațe. V: Rubricatură de carte poștală. Text imprimat în limba maghiar: „Lukova, 1915.VI.20 / Menekülő lengyelek. Kiürites / M.Z. 98 / 1934 / A. Cs. Es kir. 82 székely gyalogezred hadirokkant alapja javára” și în limba română „Secui”. Ștampilă: Baron Brukenthal`sches Museum in Hermannstadt. Număr de Inventar MCPR 914.

Fotografia de interior realizată în expoziția Muzeului Secuiesc din Șumuleu Ciuc (actualmente cartier al localității Miercurea Ciuc), județul Harghita. Imaginea este imprimată pe hârtie fotografică cu gelatino-bromură de argint (Gelatin Silver Print). Reprezintă o tânără în costum popular secuiesc, așezată la o masă. Fotografia este lipită pe coperta, de culoare bordo, a albumului realizat în 1930. Acesta cuprinde imagini din expoziție și piesele expuse. Fotografia este încadrată într-un paspartu de culoare albastră. Sub fotografie, număr de inventar MCPR 1386 și text în limba maghiară: „Csiki Szekely Muzeum / Elso Kiallitasa / Csíksomlyó 1930 PÜNKÖSDJÉN” (Micul Muzeu Secuiesc / Prima expoziție / anul 1930).

Fotografie de exterior realizată cu ocazia aniversării colonizării Banatului cu șvabi. Prezintă o paradă din centrul Timișoarei, cu călăreți în costume orășenești. Imaginea, realizată după un clișeu pe sticlă, este imprimată pe hârtie sensibilizată, format Cabinet Card prin tehnica P.O.P. În partea stângă jos a imaginii este ștanțat numele atelierului fotografic și localitatea în care activează: „Szenetra / Timișoara”. Imaginea este lipită pe un carton gros, de culoare maro. Imaginea este încadrată de un paspartu realizat cu tuș negru, cu motive stillizate. Pe verso ștampilă: Muzeul „Brukenthal” Sibiu, Nr. .... . Însemnare manuscrisă în limba română: „Aniversarea colonizării Banatului cu șvabi”. Ștampila atelierului fotografic, cu tuș roșu: „Josef Szenetra / Fotografische Kunstanstalt / Timițoara IV. / Bul. Carol I. (Hunyadistrasse) 9” (Josef Szenetra / Instituție de artă fotografică). Număr de inventar MCPR 1384.

A full length portrait of a man on a path wearing a length of fringed textile near Ugak village in western Anuakland. This man was possibly the headman of Ugak, namely Ogut-wa-Giilo.

A thatched grave-hut (duat) of a man from a noble lineage (identified as Cam-wa-Medho of the Jowatcuaa clan) surrounded by a fence stockade, located close to the village of Dibango. Nobles were buried on a platform in a deep shaft, with another platform above and a hut constructed over the top and the entrance sealed. Finally, a stockade is built around the hut. Such graves are shown respect when people pass by through removing sandals and other observances.

In the distance across the grassy plain can be seen a bank of raised ground and a line of Balanites Aegyptiaca (date) trees, the site of the royal village Umar, a residence of the younger wives of past Anuak kings without children. Oko village was where royal wives with children resided.

A group of men and three nobles seated on the ground at Kinha village (associated with the Jowatong clan). The nobles are sitting on a floor cloth due to their status, identified from the left as Abula-wa-Gilo (smoking water pipe), Anyoonya-wa-Thomo and Por-wa-Ngeenyo. Abula is noted as a noble of Kinha village, with Anyoonya residing at Udhak.

A view of a treeless floodplain during the expedition march. This sort of grassy plain is characteristic of western Anuakland south of Akobo as far as Utalo on the Oboth and Nyighum on the Akobo, and may have been taken during his march back to Akobo in May 1935.

A view of grass savannah and scattered trees, characteristic of parts of western Anuakland south of Akobo as far as Utalo on the Oboth and Nyighum on the Akobo. The photo may have been taken during his march back to Akobo in May 1935 along the Oboth river.

A collection of stones outside a deceased persons hut, in preparation for the raising of a grave mound over the burial site (mura) close by. The hut is dilapidated since the pumbó or mortuary feast at which the mound is raised is often a year or more after burial. In front of the doorway is a tuka or spirit-shrine where medicines (ngua) are invoked to ensure ancestral (spirit) favour for the inhabitants of the homestead.

A binza (identified as Kamanga) standing in a homestead in full dancing apparel, including headdress. Kamanga was initiated in the abinza corporation at the instigation of Evans-Pritchard in order to gain ethnographic information about the corporation's medicines and ritual practices.
A portrait of a youth wearing a barkcloth loincloth (bagadi) and leaning on a stick.

Widows (dekurugbo) in the foreground being ritually anointed with oil by a specially designated woman at the termination of her mourning period, when a feast is held. After a husband's death widows would have been expected to marry either his brother or another close male relative (levirate).

A tuka or spirit shrine in the centre of a homestead with medicines growing at its base and two spears leant against it. A man (identified as Kisanga) is staining a carved stool (zagbali, mbata) in the background by applying a liquid to it from a clay pot boiling on a fire.

A three-quarter length portrait of a man (identified as the Gumuz chief) wearing an arabic-style white tunic. Evans-Pritchard notes that he met a small colony of these people, who had come from western Ethiopia in small groups over the years, around Roseires. They were (and are) predominantly muslim and besides agriculture kept small numbers of cattle and other livestock. This seems to have been the first image taken by Evans-Pritchard when preparing for his Dar Fung tour of 1926.

An old grind stone containing a number of rain-making stones, marking the grave of the Bari rain-maker Jada, the great-grandfather of Ali Bey, the rain-maker met by the Seligmans in 1922. The grindstone contained four stones, one perforated, which they arranged on the side of the grindstone to photograph. They note that this grave was at the foot of Belinian hill, and that should rain fail and ceremonies at more recent rain-makers' graves not prove effective, then a ceremony would also be carried out at the grave of Jada.

An unidentified European couple in their home, in an unknown location. The photograph has been posed by Buxton in the manner of an 'interiors' magazine, with both the husband and wife adopting stereotyped gender positions within the home space in keeping with 1950s English society. A drawing of a double-bladed sacred spear (entitled "Latuka Rain-Spear") seen by the Seligmans at the circular shrine outside the house of the female rain-maker Ikang at Tarangole, the main Lotuko village. The Seligmans visited Lotuko country in the early part of 1922, and according to their diary they travelled between these villages by bicycle.

A standing group portrait of a hunter and two Mandari women, one with a breast-feeding baby and a young girl standing in front. The woman to the right is smoking a pipe and wearing a metal disk fringed goat-skin apron with two bead waist strings, as well as a cloth breast covering and bead neck ornaments. She also shows a number of scarification marks on her abdomen and arm, it being unclear whether these were intended to be decorative. The young girl is wearing a single waist string of beads and a neck ornament, a common set of ornaments for young children. The man has a goat-hair tassel attached to his arm and a goat-hair decorated quiver, bow and spear (for hunting), as well as some sort of hand weapon or ornament. He is wearing European-style shorts and no display bead strings, possibly suggesting that he is married. The women's skin skirts also suggest that they may be married, and that this may be a family group.

A full-length group portrait of three Mandari girls wearing checked textile waist-cloths, strings of neck beads (often gifted by male admirers) and single plumes in their hair. Beyond to the right can be seen a youth wearing a set of waist beads denoting an age set, and carrying a club.

A three-quarter length portrait of two young Mandari women in a cattle camp wearing yellow textile body cloths and a large number of mostly red bead strings around their waist, as well as some around the neck [partial double exposure]. Such bead strings were often given to young women by courting male youths. Youths wear such rem beads as a way of denoting their age grade grouping and for display.

A full length group portrait of five men in uniforms of the Anglo-Egyptian Condominium authority (1899-1955) wearing a belted tunic and a hat with regimental plume. Beyond them is a long stone and brick built rectilinear building with a large thatched roof, perhaps a barracks?

View of trees seen in the distance, including one especially tall or prominent tree, apparently on the edge or outskirts of Benin City. A caption below the print (written by the album's compiler) describes the place as being '[w]here the attack was made from', i.e. the direction from which the final assault by British troops on the city commenced. The caption continues: 'The big cotton tree is where the King was to be hanged.'
View of a settlement in the forest.
View of trees and vegetation just outside Benin City, captioned in black ink above the print 'The right flank'.
View of a damaged or ruined (largely destroyed) house, otherwise unidentified, in Benin City, photographed in the aftermath of the British military attack on the city.

View of the wooden framework structures of unfinished houses in the forest at the king's (Oba's) 'new bush town' (apparently located about a three-hour march from Aynie), captioned in black ink above and below the print 'The king's new bush town/ as we found it'.

Group portrait of eight men, including British officers and others, standing and sitting – identified as Lieut. O'Shea (seated on ground), Maj. Frederick Landon (sitting, left), Capt. Charles Carter (sitting, centre), Capt. Herbert Walker (sitting, right), Capt. Charles Ringer (standing, left), Lieut. John Daniels (standing, second from left), Dr. Felix Roth (standing, second from right) and Capt. Searle (standing, right) – taken inside the king's (Oba's) residence, or palace or 'compound' area, in Benin City, in the aftermath of the British military attack on the city. Clearly visible at the left of the image are a number of commemorative heads and other figures, which were in the process of being collected and removed (elsewhere described in related documentation as 'loot').

Group portrait of nine men, standing, including six British officers or members of the Niger Coast Protectorate Force (N.C.P.F.) – identified as Maj. Norman Burrows (third from left), Dr. Robert Allman (fourth from left), Capt. Charles Ringer (fifth from left), Maj. Ernest Roupell (sixth from left), Alfred Turner (third from right) and Capt. Charles Carter (right) – and three unnamed African men (soldiers or auxiliaries/porters). They are pictured in front of the king's (Oba's) residence, or palace or 'compound', in Benin City.

A head and shoulders profile portrait of one of the most important and well-known early twentieth century Luo leaders, Chief Ogada of Kisumu clan, seated on a European chair against the backdrop of the administrative building in Kisumu. His hide body covering is elaborately decorated with small beads. Ogada gave Hobley a detailed description of his personal ornaments as seen in this photograph, including stone neck beads (tik ng’ut), bead and metal earrings (ngaga) and armlets (minyonge). His cleanly shaved head is strange since chiefs covered their heads with head gear as a sign of authority. [Gilbert Oteyo 21/04/2005 &  CM 24/04/2007]

These are Luo women going fishing with fishing basket traps (osech kiteng'a - osera means 'woven fishing trap' and kiteng’a is the fishing method of covering the fish in the water with this trap, with its pointed end upwards). Kiteng'a was always a fishing method for women only. The traps are made of those ropes seen being made in 1998.209.44.1 - .2 and they are usually carried on the head like this. These women are standing probably at the entrance of their homestead, which is apparently planted with some young banana trees. Their personal body adornments include wrist bracelets (minyonge), glass neck beads (tikng’ut) and glass waist beads (tik nungo). Three of the ladies wear skin or cloth aprons (olemo) on the front while the one to the extreme right wears a fibre tail (chieno) to her rear, suggesting that they are young married women. Unmarried ladies were traditionally not keen on kiteng’a fishing, which was done mostly by married women. [Gilbert Oteyo 06/05/05]

An upper body portrait of a man (identified as Ezekiel Onyango) wearing European shirt and jacket, a stick under his left arm. Onyango was a local colonial chief living in Kadimo village in Yimbo location at the time of Evans-Pritchard's visit.

Lake Kanyaboli is a well known lake in Luo land and is mainly in Alego Location, as well as Sakwa and Yimbo Locations. The lake is a swamp lake formed by water from the River Yala. This river starts in the Western Kenya highlands and runs through most of Siaya District of Nyanza Province before emptying into a swamp also called Yala Swamp. The water tends to seep through the swamp into this lake which does not therefore allow the River Yala to actually drain into Lake Victoria. [Gilbert Oteyo 9/9/2004]

Women dancing at a funeral ceremony called tero buru (driving death away). This is usually a ceremony after burial where people shout and curse death, rigorously running and dancing to drive away bad spirits from the home of a deceased person. Although women are dancing here and one would ordinarily say that this may be a woman’s funeral, in related images to this one a large number of cattle can seen being driven beyond the women by men with shields, and it would seem therefore that this is the tero buru of a respectable elder. The dancers are all women clad in headdresses and woven dancing tails (chieno) made of vegetable fibre. Their bodies are meticulously decorated with smears of soil or ochre of varying colours. [Gilbert Oteyo 9/9/2004]

This is a view of a Luo settlement earthwork called gunda bur (gunda being a abandoned home, bur the bank and ditch). People lived within the earthwork where houses were built and cattle were tethered, protected by the bank and ring-ditch (created by the excavation of earth to build up the bank). These structures were built by the Luo at the beginning of the 1700s and some remained occupied until the late 1800s. In the original notes, this photo is described as the 'old bur Asembo' and I am inclined to think that this is one of the old settlement locations of the Asembo clan. Many of these spectacular earthworks still exist in Asembo location up to this present day. [Gilbert Oteyo 9/9/2004 & CM 16/03/2007]

A snap-shot of a Luo man wearing a traditional woven hat on which is stuck a number of warthog teeth (lak njiri) and probably a hippo tooth (lak rawo). Another hippo tooth hangs from the neck across his chest. The man's neck is heavily adorned by glass bead necklaces (tik ngut) and he is also wearing cowrie shell decoration over his hand. This man is certainly an elder of status, and may be dressed for a ceremony. [Gilbert Oteyo 9/9/2004 & CM 16/03/2007]

This is an earthwork of a typical Luo defended homestead enclosure dating to the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. The dug ditch and bank structure is called bur in Luo, and an abandoned home is gunda, which gives the term gunda bur for this type of archaeological earthwork. People lived within the earthwork, where houses were built and cattle tethered, protected by both the earthwork and the surrounding ring ditch. In the original notes, this photo is described as the 'old bur Asembo' and I am inclined to think that this is one of the old earthwork settlements of the Asembo clan of the Luo. Many of these spectacular earthworks still exist in Asembo Location up to day. [Gilbert Oteyo 9/9/2004 & CM 23/03/2007]

A Luo warrior (or just a man going to a funeral) holding a spear and a hide shield. An animal hide/skin lap (pien) is hanging below the bottom of the shield. On his head is a Colobus monkey tail headdress (kondo bim). This attire is usually for warriors and those going to a funeral as they will perform the funeral ceremony tero buru there. Curious children are watching from behind. [Gilbert Oteyo 9/9/2004]

This man is dressed in a long robe (kanzu or kandho) and wears a glass bead decorated hat (ogut tigo). This hat is only worn by men and not by women. Around his waist is a belt, probably of sisal fibre (okanda tworo), and he is holding his walking stick (luth) under his arm. On his feet he is wearing sandals made of animal hide or skin (wuoche pien). He is playing a wind instrument (oporo) which is made of animal horn at one end, and attached to a long hollow wood or bamboo pipe which he blows on the side. Such an instrument is usually played during funerals but also during other entertainment ceremonies. [Gilbert Oteyo 9/9/2004]
A group portrait of three men from Kogelo Clan (Jokogelo) in Alego Location. Their names are not given but they look very Westernized from their clothing. [Gilbert Oteyo 9/9/2004]

Lui Junior Secondary School written in English and Arabic outside the school compound. Two huts and a building can be seen in the distance. The school was built in 1975 by the Sudan Council of Churches. The first school was opened in Lui by Dr, Frazer, a missionary, who brought Christianity to the area in the 1920's, built a church, a school and a hospital in the area, and brought peace as well. Between 1965-72, during the civil war, the Moru Misa people scattered into the hills, and were only just settling back again when we visited. Some still hadn't returned. Patti Langton [28/07/2009]

An image of a gourd used as a dance rattle, GARA. It is placed on the ground to be photographed  in informant Deborah's compound. It is hollowed out and filed with sorghum seeds, and cassava leaves stuffed in the neck. The traditional rattle dance, still enacted from 9pm to morning, for ceremonies. Women use the rattles and dance in the inner circle, while the men, without rattles, dance in the outer circle the opposite way. These days the rattles are also used in Church, and at dances on Friday night. Patti Langton [23/03/2009]

In the informant Deborah's compound there is an area for graves. They are set in a circle, each one different. Deborah had 6 sisters and 3 brothers. 3 sisters died as babies, and at least one as an adult. This grave belongs to an aunt.  The megalith faces west as she was female. The stones are piled to a height of about 100cm and the megalith is 199cm high. You can see the outline of the triangular heap of stones denoting a leper's grave directly behind.  Patti Langton [23/03/2009]

This is a Mangaviri trap for capturing small animals like gazelle. There is a tree trunk bent over sticks. A noose is hanging from it down to almost ground level. Decoratively carved grave marker by a roadside. It has KHARALA carved on the top (see image 2008.78.2.40). This is one of a number of old wooden grave markers along the road from Mundri to Amadi.  A village can be seen behind. The road-builders moved the road specially to avoid them. Informant Andrea told us that these grave markers were used before the current style of  graves as seen in informant Deborah's compound (see 2008.78.1.38). Deborah's account of them was that grave markers were used when there was no body, if the family member had died far away - to bring the 'soul' home. This grave marker has three 'rings' carved at the top. There used to be specialist craftsmen who made the grave markers. Patti Langton [26/05/2009]

Two carvings, one with horn-shaped elongations, tallying the numbers of large animals killed by the person buried beneath, or sometimes the kills of a relative. Graves were commonly grouped together near a settlement (visible in the background). These carvings were understood as a means of honouring the dead but did not have any particular ritual meaning.

A long wooden rain-post (riyak) stuck into the ground under a large tree with a shorter notched post (lingi) for hunting-magic offerings, usually fowl sacrifice. During drought the rain-post was the focus for rain-making rituals involving the sprinkling of durra (Sorghum bicolor) over an assembled crowd by a rain-maker (biriak).

Two carved wooden funerary figures, one with large horns set on top of a low earth burial mound within a homestead with a large well-thatched crop storage hut raised on piles behind, called a gallotoh by Schweinfurth. Not all Bongo graves were marked with a mound of stones, and such mounds were sometimes erected a number of years later at a mortuary ceremony. These carved figures were considered representations of the deceased, put up to honour the individual, but not serving any ritual purpose. Usually accompanied by tallies of animals killed in hunting, the horns on the figure signify the status of the hunter.

A long wooden rain-post (riyak) with maize heads and medicines attached, stuck into the ground under a large nilotic shea-butter tree, Vitellaria paradoxa ssp. nilotica, a slow-growing hardwood fruit tree indigenous to northern Uganda and Southern Sudan. During drought this post was the focus for rain-making rituals involving the sprinkling of durra (Sorghum bicolor) over an assembled crowd by a rain-maker (biriak).

Two carved wooden funerary figures, one with large horns set on top of a low earth burial mound within a homestead. Not all Bongo graves were marked with a mound of stones, and such mounds were sometimes erected a number of years later at a mortuary ceremony. These carved figures were considered representations of the deceased, put up to honour the individual, but not serving any ritual purpose. Usually accompanied by tallies of animals killed in hunting, the horns on the figure signify the status of the hunter [image cloudy at top].

A stone mound near a hut erected over a man's grave (dodo) with three carved posts surmounting the top tallying twenty elephants killed in the hunt by the deceased, placed as a means of honouring him. Around the mound are five more carved posts (some with arrows stuck in them); the first a likeness of the deceased, the next clockwise a forked (horn-shaped) post set up by his son-in-law yet tallying his own buffalo kills. The next (only tip visible) is a likeness of the deceased with a tally of two hippo killed, then a forked post tallying six rhino and lastly a forked post tallying five buffalo.

A horizon of savannah, with smoke rising from grass-firing. Evans-Pritchard took numerous photographs of vegetation to document changes in the cattle-keeping environment during his fieldwork. The firing of grass was done to promote new shoots for cattle to eat during the dry season.

A clay ox as made by Nuer children, complete with pendant horn ornaments, placed on a stool standing on a table with papers scattered on it. The room in which the photograph is taken looks out through a large window onto a courtyard with an overhanging corrugated iron roof and a woven grass perimeter fence, seen as a backdrop in other object images. It is likely to be the American Mission station at Nasir.
A dark image of a youth with hands raised to his face, standing next to a large woodfuel pile for steamers on the Sobat River.

A head-and-shoulders portrait of a man wearing a body-cloth with feather hair decoration [poor focus], standing next to the Sobat River. Evans-Pritchard notes that this man could be an Anuak, but his initiation scars suggest that he is Nuer.
A head-and-shoulders profile portrait of a youth, standing next to the Sobat River [dark image].

A slightly distant view of a herd of cattle comprising a cattle camp, set in a wide expanse of treeless grass savannah in western Nuerland. It is probable that this is a very early dry season camp without huts being made, which fits with Evans-Pritchard's 1936 fieldwork which straddled the end of the rains with the beginning of the dry season. This may relate to the early November camp from Nyueny village described by Evans-Pritchard in one of his articles.

A clay ox as made by Nuer children, complete with large hump and ash markings, placed on a stool with a woven grass perimeter fence as a backdrop. In other images it is clear that this was a courtyard fence at a mission or government property, most likely at Nasir.

A riek spirit-shrine post in the foreground set in the earth near a hut, with a reed fence beyond. Near it is a swept area with ?mat rolls placed around it and a pile of stones in the middle. The hut is made from mopane poles lashed together in a meshwork and plastered in between with soil from termite mounds (mmu wa seolo).

Hut for visitors, goods, etc., in the plot of Kashiate Mogumbula, an Mbukushu woman living in Boseja ward. She was born in Angola who moved with her parents to Etsha 3, gradually moving to Maun and this ward. She stated that she only found people building like this, using dithupa (a meshwork of sticks) packed with earth, here in Boseja. It seemed to her to be a very localised style in this ward due to difficulties of accessing mud bricks or money for concrete bricks, or money for letlhaka.

View of a large stone carving at the ancient Maya site of Quirigua located near the banks of the Motagua river in the department of Izabal, Guatemala. The photograph shows the east side of a carved stone zoomorph known by archaeologists as Zoomorph B, as it was first described by Alfred Maudslay in his seminal publication of the Quirigua site in his multi-volume Archaeology (1889–1902): 'This monument is lying on three large slabs of stone, which are well shown in Plates IX [ie. this photograph] and X. It is carved into the shape of a great dragon, with a human head, bust, and hands issuing from the dragon's mouth. In Plate XII, a, the two great eyes of the dragon, with hanging eyelashes and crossed bands over the eyeballs, can be clearly seen. The upper jaw is raised so that the row of incisor teeth shows above the grotesque mask which surmounts the human head.' More recent scholarship dates the zoomorph (also known as Monument 2) to 9.17.10.0.0, 12 Ahau 8 Pax (Maya calendar), or A.D. 780 in the standard Western (Gregorian) calendar. Identified over the years variously as a tiger, dragon, turtle and toad, the carving is now understood by scholars to represent a supernatural crocodilian, sometimes termed the Cosmic Monster. The monument was created during the later part of the sixty-year reign of K'ak' Tiliw Chan Yopaat and marked the close of an era in the Maya calendar. It was one of a number of stelae and zoomorphs erected at Quirigua as part of a complex building programme which took place at the height of the city-state's power during the Late Classic period, and whose primary aim was to legitimate and reinforce the power of the ruler.

View of a large stone carving at the ancient Maya site of Quirigua located near the banks of the Motagua river in the department of Izabal, Guatemala. The photograph shows the north face of a carved stone zoomorph known by archaeologists as Zoomorph P, as it was first described by Alfred Maudslay in his seminal publication of the Quirigua site in his multi-volume Archaeology (1889–1902): 'This great monument, which must weigh nearly twenty tons, stands, like the other monolithic animals, on a foundation of three large flat stones, which are not visible in the photographs. When first found it presented a most enigmatic appearance, for it was not until the earth had been dug away around the base that the great hands or flippers could be seen, which proved the main design to be the representation of a great turtle. The head of the animal, which faces nearly south, is surrounded by a hieroglyphic inscription. [...] The north face of the monument is in the form of a serpent's or dragon's head with a human figure seated cross-legged within its widely-opened jaws.' More recent scholarship dates the zoomorph (also known as Monument 16) to 9.18.5.0.0, 4 Ahau 13 Ceh (Maya calendar), or A.D. 795 in the standard Western (Gregorian) calendar. Identified over the years as various different animals, the carving is now understood by scholars to represent a Cosmic Monster with a mountain on its back. The monument was created during the reign of Sky Xul and marked the close of an era in the Maya calendar. It was one of a number of stelae and zoomorphs erected at Quirigua as part of a complex building programme which took place during the Late Classic period, and whose primary aim was to legitimate and reinforce the power of the ruler.

View of a large stone carving at the ancient Maya site of Quirigua located near the banks of the Motagua river in the department of Izabal, Guatemala. The photograph shows the east side of a carved stone stela known by archaeologists as Stela C, as it was first described by Alfred Maudslay in his seminal publication of the Quirigua site in his multi-volume Archaeology (1889–1902): 'In size and general appearance this monument closely resembles Stela A. The principal differences are: - That four glyphs form a pedestal to the figures carved on the front and back of the monument instead of a grotesque mask. On the front of the monument the two faces in profile near the top are grotesque instead of human faces. [...] The back of the monument is broader than the front.' More recent scholarship dates the stela (also known as Monument 3) to 9.17.5.0.0 (Maya calendar), or A.D. 775 in the standard Western (Gregorian) calendar. The monument was created during the later part of the sixty-year reign of K'ak' Tiliw Chan Yopaat and marked the close of an era in the Maya calendar. It was one of a number of stelae and zoomorphs erected at Quirigua as part of a complex building programme which took place at the height of the city-state's power during the Late Classic period, and whose primary aim was to legitimate and reinforce the power of the ruler.

View of a large stone carving at the ancient Maya site of Quirigua located near the banks of the Motagua river in the department of Izabal, Guatemala. The photograph shows the east side of a carved stone stela known by archaeologists as Stela F, as it was first described by Alfred Maudslay in his seminal publication of the Quirigua site in his multi-volume Archaeology (1889–1902): 'This is the most graceful and most elaborately decorated of all the Quirigua stelae. [...] The graceful arrangement of the feather-work on the upper part of this monument is well worthy of note.' More recent scholarship dates the stela (also known as Monument 6) to 9.16.10.0.0, 1 Ahau 3 Zip (Maya calendar), or A.D. 761 in the standard Western (Gregorian) calendar. Considered to be one of the great masterpieces of Mesoamerican sculpture, the monument was created during the later part of the sixty-year reign of K'ak' Tiliw Chan Yopaat and marked the close of an era in the Maya calendar. It was one of a number of stelae and zoomorphs erected at Quirigua as part of a complex building programme which took place at the height of the city-state's power during the Late Classic period, and whose primary aim was to legitimate and reinforce the power of the ruler.

View of a Zuni shrine.  According to James Stevenson's original note for this photograph (prepared circa 1885), '[t]hese shrines are usually situated on the summit of some distant mesa or mountain in some mythic and secluded spot where it is least likely to be molested by intruders.  The Zunis are devoted shrine worshippers.  Eight of these shrines are situated at a distance from Zuni, in different directions, and are annually visited by the various religious orders of the tribe when the season arrives for the deposit of a new god.  These visits are attended with peculiar ceremonies.  When the shrine is thus visited the old god is displaced, removed to the rear, and a new one planted in its stead.  As the picture shows, these successive visits have produced quite a large pile of deposed deities.'

View of buildings at Zuni pueblo, located on the Rio Zuni river (a tributary of the Little Colorado), with a building in the foreground.  According to James Stevenson's original note for this photograph (prepared circa 1885), Zuni 'is the most renowned village in all the pueblo group.  It is by far the largest and most typical in every respect.'

Portrait of a woman, kneeling on a blanket on the ground, polishing the inside of a large clay pot with a smooth pebble.  According to James Stevenson's original note for this photograph (prepared circa 1885), '[a]fter the piece of pottery to be polished is completed and sun-dried, it is taken into the house, a quantity of the same material of which the vessel is made is thoroughly pulverized, and made into a solution, and after all the coarse or gritty substances are removed from it by straining, the solution is applied to the surface of the vessel by means of a rabbit-skin mop.  It is then rubbed with the stone, and the application repeated until the desired smoothness and polish is obtained.  The vessel is again thoroughly sun-dried, and is then ready for the kiln.  Pottery on which it is intended to paint designs is manipulated in the same manner, but no polishing-stone is used after the vessel is decorated.'

Portrait of a Zuni woman, standing, carrying a large decorated pottery vessel on her head.  According to James Stevenson's original note for this photograph (prepared circa 1885), the photograph depicts 'a Zuni squaw, holding a water-vase on the top of the head, just as they appear while carrying water from the well to the house.  This is a fair specimen of the Zuni woman as she appears in her daily tasks.  The bulky, clumsy leggings form part of the moccasins.  A long buck-skin strip about four inches wide which is attached to the moccasin is wrapped around the leg nearly to the knee, each layer slightly over-lapping the other, the end being tightly inserted beneath the last layer of buckskin to hold it in place.  The gown is woven from native yarn dyed black or dark blue with a vegetable dye.  The garment is first made as a blanket, nearly square; the ends are then sewed together, one side being left open.  This open end forms the bottom of the dress, while apertures are made in the other for the head and arms.  One shoulder is left partly exposed while the other is beneath the dress.'

View of several Zuni people standing with laden donkeys (burros).  According to James Stevenson's original note for this photograph (prepared circa 1885), '[i]t will be observed that the men and squaws both take part in the labo[u]r and carry almost as large and heavy loads as the donkey.  The scene represents a family just as it has returned from the field.'

Portrait of five men standing in front of a house. One is wearing an apron decorated with cowrie shells in two blocks, three stripes and a zigzag line and ear ornaments with long strings. He and the other men are wearing neck ornaments of two pairs of boars' tusks with shell plates and cornelian beads, and necklaces of long tubular shells. On their wrists are cylindrical ornaments of cane covered with cowrie shells and with a bristly edge of short goat hair, and on their arms thick ivory armlets indicating high status. Two men are smoking brass pipes. Three of them wear fringed body cloths. In the background stands a tall bamboo pole with a tuft of leaves tied to it.

The eastern courtyard, Deyang shar, of the Potala palace. Two rings of masked dancers are performing a ritual dance. The dancers of the outer circle are wearing black hats, shva nag, and those of the inner circle are wearing animal masks. Two monks are standing in the centre (to the left of the scene) with a small table between them on which ritual implements have been placed.  A tiger-skin carpet is on the ground in front of them. The enthroned figure (behind which spectators are gathered) is a masked representation of Chinese priest Hashang who presides over the dance. There is an appliquéd awning to the right of the scene where a monk orchestra is seated on padded seats. An open parapet provides an upper viewpoint for spectators. This ceremony was part of the New Year celebrations possibly taking place on the 29th day of the 12th month, the votive offering of the twenty ninth day, Tse gutor.

View of several Konyak Naga men, probably of the village of Longmien (now Longmeang), wearing only tight belts, carrying bags and baskets slung over their shoulders, and in the foreground several men working on the ground, possibly digging or reaping.

'Konyak / Divided heads from Namsang' (handwritten caption). View of divided skulls from Namsang kept as tropies by Konyak Naga men, suspended from a horizontal bamboo pole.  From left to right: the left side of the skull, given to the 'second spear' (if three men are in at the death); the back, given to the 'third spear' (if three men) or the 'second spear' (if two men); the right half, given to the 'first spear' (if three men); and the whole front, given to the first spear (if two men).

'Konyak / House of chief of Yansa' (handwritten caption). View of several Konyak Naga people standing outside and inside a large building identified as the house of the chief of the village of Yansa/Yanha (now called Joboka), with a thatched roof supported by wooden pillars, and with woven panels as outer walls, decorated with mithan (ox) horns and other objects.

'Konyak / Young men of Longkong' (handwritten caption). Full-length portrait of two young Konyak Naga men, from Longkong or possibly from Zusa, with other Naga people sitting behind them on a raised platform.  Both men are wearing plumed headdresses, ear ornaments, loincloths secured at the waist with several thick rings or cords, many bangles at their wrists, many beaded necklaces, and a carved figure of a human head hanging on their chests; one is holding a dao (cutting implement) and a woven basket with beaded tassels, the other is holding a cloak or blanket.
'Konyak, / Defences of Longkong' (handwritten caption). View of a soldier holding a rifle with bayonet, standing beside palisades with panjis (sharpened stakes) at the village of Longkong.

'Konyak of Saochu (?) / or Tobu side / Hutton' (handwritten caption). Half-length portrait of a Konyak Naga man tentatively identified as either from the village of Saochu (now called Sauchu, described by Hutton elsewhere as 'a Konyak village of the sub-tribe called Chagyik by the Changs') or from the neighbouring village of Tobu. He has a tattooed line straight down the middle of his face and wears tasseled ear ornaments and a neck ornament of boar's tusks.

Originally it was either completed or planned to consist of three gothic arches built with enormous blocks of stone, but only one such arch remains and the others either collapsed in construction or afterwards and are now spanned by huge flat slabs, the footway being carried down to the flat slabs by steps from the arch top.' (tour diary, 21 October 1925)

View of a pool with stone walls, probably the one between Syndai and Jaintiapur (now Jaintapur) described by Hutton as follows: 'A little further on is a tank cut entirely out of solid rock with gutter and drains likewise excavated out of the rock to bring the rain water from the slope above it to keep it full. The tank is 22'11" broad by 29'2" long round the edge and descends inside in three broad steps, the depth in the centre being 6' from the bottom to the level of the outer edge.' (tour diary, 22 October 1925)

Sincu. Cheese mould made by Panare for local peasants. Flat woven mat with chevron design, rolled and tied with synthetic string.

Wapa, or basketry tray. Round, shallow tray, with woven geometric design in black and light brown. The outer edge of the tray is supported with a cane ring frame on the top and bottom, tied on with fibre.
Tawahemen. Woven black and white basket with circular rim and square base. Cane around rim, attached with fibre string. Traditional Panare design.
Wooden cooking spatula with flat paddle; straight sides and rounded end. The handle is flat and narrow with a flaring terminal.

Wapa. A shallow, round tray made from plaited basketry with frames of cane attached by fibre to the inside and outside of the rim. Plaited black and natural geometric pattern with two central rows of dog motifs within squares. Small loop of fibre attached to the frame.

Oyaru or back pack with wooden frame and woven back, possibly of leather. Furred hide straps attached in four places, knotted together in two places. There are also bark straps attached in four places. The leather, bark and hide straps are stiff and frayed in places. There are two dark stains; one in the centre of the pack, and one at the top, which extends to the bark strap.
Manioc press. An imitation or model made for tourists, some canes painted black and red. Attachment loop at one end, two openings through the opposite end.
Dance belt made of tree bark and decorated with a black pigment in a diamond pattern.
Small model of a rush basket. Stake and strand type, 'X' shaped supporting bars with straight straights woven between them. One area form the rim broken and missing.
Barberry wood crab catcher with a four pronged head, wooden dowels and fibrous binding.
Narrow woven belt with twisted fringe at each end. Woven with alternating red and white stripes.

Tamshi: from which baskets are made by peeling off bark and splitting. Doesn't grow at Pomara and have to travel 10 miles to Montenegro to find this creeper. Long length of thick vine coiled into a bundle, ridged.
Choochooas, quinina or quinine collected from wild trees. Grated and added to distilled sugar juice (aguacaliente) and then left for a week. Boiled when liquid turns pink and taken one cup a day.

Humberta. Small bird skin of a Green Honeycreeper with teal and green feathers, stuffed with cotton. Eyes have been removed, and the beak is in place. One leg and some feathers are detached but present.

Basin shaped basket, with redbud bark and dogwood stem sewing on mixed foundation of dogwood splints and three rod bundle. Used for parching seeds with hot coals, sometimes also used for cooking acorn mush by stone boiling.

Gamuts. Woman’s headdress of black velvet decorated with pig or boar tusks. Central row of cowrie shells stitched along front with bands of pink, blue, green and yellow glass beads above and below, arranged into geometric patterns. Decorative metal chain stitched along front top and bottom. At front centre, three groups of outward pointing tusks: four tusks at centre, and three tusks in groups either side. Tusks wrapped in vertical black velvet bands with rows of red, yellow, green and white beads. Two mustard-yellow synthetic ties either side with further tassels below, stitched on reverse, in green, black, blue, mustard and red. Reverse also black velvet.

Jar; lid - A: A carved wooden jar, modelled on a traditional form of earthenware jar - ngatsi - used to contain rice wine. The upper part is carved with human figures with legs raised on either side of the torso. There are two vertical and three horizontal protuberances in form of bones. Possibly decorative or as vestigial handles. Condition fair: Several cracks at the base, including two major ones. B: The wooden lid depicts a coiled snake. Condition fair: Abrasions and a hole visible at one side.

A rectangular textile made from multiple squares and rectangles of red, yellow and green silk. They are embroidered with tree and floral motif in various coloured threads, with small tassels across the textile; there are long purple cords attached near the centre, with silk tassels and white shells at the ends. Possibly a tabard.

Round teapot, designed to be used for the preparation of gongfu tea. The seal on the base reads 'Taozhong', and the one under the lid reads 'Ge' (respectively the given name and family name of the artist). Pot and lid made from fine, dark brown pottery, there is an etched inscription in Chinese characters. The inscription says that the pot given to the Museum by the artist, gives the name of the material (zisha), says that the design was adapted from a traditional design and that the pot was made entirely by hand, and gives the production date (Spring 2004) and the name of the artist.

The teapot, 2004.184 A-B, is packed in its own box with tissue paper. The box is cardboard with a textured exterior. Inside the bottom of the box and the underside of the lid are padded squares of bright yellow synthetic silk. The upper square has an orange ribbon across one corner. The front of the box has been damaged by the removal of adhesive tape.
A purple synthetic velvet liner. A pad covered with purple synthetic velvet on one side and bright yellow synthetic silk on the other, with a red silk ribbon for removal.
Pat'i. A woven woollen belt made by Sherbegum. It is yellow and green with black geometric designs and tassels. Part of a Kalasha costume.
Box - Lime box made from the tip of a horn, with wooden stopper
Bhodd. Man's traditional shirt. Made of fine, machine-woven cotton.

Pro. Red, velvet shawl. Everyday item of woman's clothing, worn with knot over the left shoulder. Worn by Pa-chyu during the most dangerous part of rituals in remembrance of a powerful female Pa-chyu.
Phahsa; Ri Saida Saimain; Ta; Thahlen; Me; Khohre; Mhachyorhim; Khohja; Karda; Sanaso.
Armband - Bronze armlet, decorated all over with engraved designs
Earring - Women's brass earrings. A bundle of rings, each about 18" diameter.
"Lunch basket", comprising two halves which form top and bottom.
Portrait sculpture in plaster by Marguerite Milward, of Mila, a 25 year-old man from the Newar community, working as a gardener in Kathmandu.
One of a pair of large carved book covers. "Probably made by Newar craftsmen in Nepal. Examples of this covering are not common as the art is no longer practised." (Note by C.J.M., 8th June 1931)

A man's long coat made of blue cotton, with a grey lining. The coat has a high neck and wrap closure that is fastened loops made of orange braiding and with gold coloured metal buttons that are attached at the ends of lengths of orange braiding.
Bös. Green silk sash, with repeating geometric pattern in the weft.

Cotton collar. Flat and curved with flat ends; formed of black cotton with zigzag pattern on exterior, with a black silk trim along the inner curve and short sides, bordered by metallic strip with green and pink thread, and a blue silk strip. The interior has pink-red cotton with navy blue stitching along outer curve.
Costume. Silver neck clasp, with ?turquoise and coral settings.

Copper alloy, probably brass bowl, used for rice. The decoration on the interior of the bowl appears to have been made with a comb and consists of horizontal lines going around the edge of the rim, with semi-circles and vertical strips around the edge and a floral decoration in the centre of the piece.
Wooden guard to protect hand from rope when crossing native bridges.
Cloth, of undyed woven cotton, rectangular in shape, made up of two pieces sewn together, long edges of each piece with single stripe of blue.
Portrait sculpture of Kuju, a nineteen year-old Sora man,
Canework comb. Non-ceremonial, and worn by ordinary tribesmen.

Ãepiec. Woman's cap. The body of the cap has embroidered patterns in pink, red, yellow, purple, green, and blue. The top of the cap is made of a red fabric with embroidered and lace decorations, and a woven panel is sewn to the bottom.
Zastera. Woman's apron. The apron is white with woven and embroidered motifs in pink, orange, purple, green, and blue, with floral designs. The apron is bordered by ribbons and hemmed with lace.
White lace strip with blue edging.
A piece of cloth with embroidered patterns in red, blue, and yellow. Possibly a piece of an unfinished cap.

One miniature fur parka for a doll made from several pieces of brown fur and white fur. The pieces are sewn together and decorated with green, yellow, red, and blue fabric appliqué. It has no sleeves.
Blackthorn pins. Used for securing the blankets covering tents.
Two small, wooden clothes peg charms.

Pocket sundial ('shepherd's' sundial). Comprises a turned wood column, marked around its circumference with red-inked incised lines, numbers and letters for determining the time according to the month, surmounted by an onion-shaped stopper with concealed folding gnomon, with a small iron suspension loop at the top to which is affixed a long length of pink string. The stopper is now very firmly stuck in place.

Tamata. Votive offering. Large nose made from green wax. Hand modelled cone shape with two indentations on the wider end to represent nostrils. A string loop on the narrower end suggests a point of suspension.
Silver plastic protective disc-shaped charm placed on car dashboard. Representation of St. Christopher on obverse. Simulated leather on reverse.
Tamata. Votive offering of a kidney, stamped on thin, silver sheet metal. Detail incised around the outline. There is a semicircular tab and hole for attachment of a pin.

Riessasilki. Scarf, made by Aino Kitti, composed of white, machine-woven, nylon textile that has an embossed pattern of roses. Square shaped, with a looped fringe along all four edges. Made for a woman.

Container made from red gum wood, coloured red and covered on the exterior with a trellis like design made of engraved wavy lines. Larger examples are used for food gathering or even water carrying. A large, shallow variety, called "koolamon", is used for carrying babies, the women holding them in the curve of the arm

Almost triangular openwork wooden board carved with distinct face at top and 4 hook prongs, 2 each side of central bar, near base. Capped headtop above central piercing, and oval painted in middle of forehead. Concentric oval ring eyes, club nose with crescentic nostrils or base, oval mouth. Chevron cheek marks, connected with eye (?). Main body panel carved with single pair of birds with vertically interlocking tails in centre. Additional birds at each corner, top birds lie right up next to face. Between corner birds along sides are lobefaces.

Double thick overcoiled curved cane rod with scalloped wicker frame on underside of curve and rectangular bark covered plate in centre. Long red overcoiled tail issues from tapered base of plate, pair of twisted fibre tassels are also attached. Halo of curved spikes round edge of plate framing enemy portrait head 1935.10C. 9 halo spikes have conical pith ornaments, painted red, attached. Bark piece red with white curves painted on it. Prongs broken, paint worn. Original accession notes: " Dance ornament worn suspended from waist and ornamenting buttocks. cf. 1935.8, 1935.10A/C." Poor
Lens-shaped wooden head with face carved both sides, small pierced cap with fibre and reed string through piercing. Made of pale light wood, stained a darker black/brown.

Necklace made from plaited string work in form of face with long tail at chin, bulbous forehead, loops for ears at sides, and short angled tails below the ears. Cowrie shells under forehead for eyes. Ribbed nose-loop with 2 irridescent shell hook spirals and single curved boar's tusk sliver through loop as nose ornament. Face attached to overcoiled fastening strings, one of which has large knot near its ends the other an overcoiled loop. Fibre binding ties nose ornaments together, pith padding strip holds them in place in nose loop. String work blackened on face, except for chin tail.

Arrow with three blackened, curved wooden points bound together near base with cane. All three have small, widely spaced alternate side barbs. No foreshaft. Shaft binding of diagonally crossed cane over coiled bast fibre. Tapering bamboo shaft stained red.

Na’u Nangk-Au. Rounded necked red earthenware jar for sago with applique face on one side of neck representing the mythical woman Demwo-Kwo-Nembit who visited Aibom in her canoe bringing dancers. Mended but still very fragile.

Paint-tray. Flat bottomed shallow ovoid bowl with rat head at one end and rough ovoid pierced tail at the other. Red paint on outside in incisions of geometrical design of ovals and curves, faint red paint on base. Original accession notes: " Animal head handle, represents MGMUT PE (rat)." Good
Carinated bowl with single handle supporting an upright projection. Interior and upper shoulder of bowl glazed with a deep red brown glaze and deeper linear decoration.
A necklace made of polished seeds; spherical black interspersed with 24 biconical red Abrus precatorius seeds.
A necklace made of spherical brown seeds with vertical ridges. Some of the seeds have small holes on the surface.

Knife with a metal blade and wooden handle. The blade is large and leaf shaped, decorated on one side of the blade with grooves; there is a circular hole near the handle end. The handle is short and flared at both terminals. A small portion of the blade edge has come away and is missing.
Large pot of burnished red ware. Everted rim, tall and narrow neck, rounded body and flat base. Decorated with linear patterns below neck, incised with pointed stick. Black firing marks on base.

Globular pot of orange clay with a flat base and narrow neck. Below the neck is a band of vertical grooves and notched pendant triangles. Upon the base and shoulder are blackened areas. The neck and rim are missing.
Two bird arrows with head ends tapered to a point. [C] has a leaf fletching, and [D] is decorated at the terminal with spiral grooves. Both are darkened at the tip; possible charring.
Black clay pipe bowl. Decorated with two horizontal bands of vertical grooves, separated by two double grooves around the circumference. Small slit in the pipe stem socket.

A rectangular piece of cloth made from two pieces of white cotton textile stitched together, both woven with vertical thin grey stripes and horizontally with thick pink and grey stripes along the top. It is embroidered with rectangular panels of geometric pattern in grey and pink threads. The edges are stitched over on two corners.
Portrait sculpture in plaster of Melthurse, a Toda man.

Male funerary ornament. Armlet or bracelet of core wrapped in red and dark blue twine, decorated with red faceted gems, possibly coloured glass, encircled by small bronze coloured seed beads, probably glass. Attached to the circlet is a large disc ornament, made of plant fibre, possibly cane, wrapped in blue thread and embellished with beads, probably glass, of silver, green, yellow and blue arranged in a geometric pattern.
Flute  - A) cane flute, with five stops (but lacking reed) and two side-shoots left as handles. B) piece of a horn, described by donor as the top part of a Toda instrument. Does not fit A very well

Jacket made of velvet and cotton, decorated with metal embellishments. Upper body of dark red velvet lined with purple woven cloth; lower body of unlined white calico or linen; short sleeves decorated with mirrors, sequins, metal sunburst motifs and glass beads on a background of woven purple, pink and metallic threads; sleeves and collar trimmed with green; five metal snap fasteners along front opening.

A necklace consisting of faceted gold gilt beads and dangling disc shapes with round projections, strung onto a length of green cotton cord. It is fastened at the ends by a loop of green cord and a gold gilt bead.

Necklace with gold filigree pendants and wooden beads. Central section consists of 20 filigree pendants made from a wire-wrapped core with decoration of wire and granulation; pendants alternate with two faceted beads with wire and granulation; section at either end of the necklace has alternating wooden beads and knots; strung on brown silk or cotton cord with a metal spring ring fastening. Three wooden beads missing.

Pennanular gilded brass armlet. Made from sheet metal, rolled over at the edges to create a hollow tubular shape; protruding pyramidal forms around the outer surface; gilded on the outer surface. One of four armlets, 1944.22.6.13-16.

Cotton bag; body of bag square in shape and with alternating red and black stripes decorated with yellow stitching in zigzag patterns; strap handle and outer edges of bag made from one continuous piece of material and ends with multicoloured tassels at the two bottom corners of the bag, decorated with embroidered geometric patterns in red and yellow.
Ear Ornament  - Ear stick worn by young men in holes made on the lobes of the ear
Necklace comprising strings of green, black, yellow and white beads on red thread. Worn by young men and women.
Arrow, the shaft is made from a long light cylindrical piece of cane, half of which has been damaged by woodworm and is missing. The head is iron with a collar, stepped shoulders and tapering point.

Simple bow with slight recurve. Wooden bow with circular cross-section tapering towards either end; iron spiral at one end; wide leather band around bow, possible grip. Lighter area of wood indicating missing leather strip.
Twaliot. Metal conical cowbell, suspended upon a plaited leather looped strap, with a cylindrical clapper. There is evidence of historic wear.

Korket. A hearth. Carved wooden stick, one side is flat and the other is rounded. The flat side has two holes at one end, the other end tapers to a point. The two holes show evidence of fire damage; caused by the friction of a drill. Poinik (fire-stick) consists of a korket (hearth) used with a kirkit (drill) to start a fire by hand through surface friction.
Kirkit. A wooden drill used with a korket (hearth) to start a fire by hand. The drill is long and cylindrical in shape with rounded ends that show signs of fire.

A dark blue wool coat with long sleeves and a long body with a full skirt. The coat has a pointed lapel, breast pocket, two side pockets with pointed pocket flaps, which are all trimmed with blue cotton; the collar is covered in black velvet. There are three shell buttons on both sides of the front opening, and no button holes; two shell buttons on both sleeve cuffs. The coat is lined with striped black and grey cloth, possibly brushed cotton; internal pocket on the proper right side.
Lapudzi. Pair of woollen socks knitted with a ribbed cuff in stripes of navy, purple, black, white and green with zigzags of bright green and pink. Tied together.
Lapudzi. Pair of woollen socks knitted with a ribbed cuff in stripes of blue, black, orange, maroon, green and pink. Tied together.
Wooden paddle with cylindrical handle and flat, straight-sided blade.

Cylindrical, double-ended wooden drum, that has been coloured with a red/brown pigment. There is a hide skin on both ends, which are held taut with netted and 'Y' shaped lacing around the body of the drum, that connects the two skins to each other. A hide strap, with a plant fibre string attached, runs along the body of the drum tied on at the top and bottom.
Tortoise shell bell. At the top and base of the head area are two circular perforations and one circular indent upon the top. There is evidence of damage at the tail end.
Ornament to be worn in the hair. Circular disc of leather with a spiral of glass beads stitched to it; blue, translucent red, pink and opaque white beads.
Iron razor blade. Roughly triangular with loop at the point.

Nyetubot. Short stabbing spear with a wooden shaft and metal spearhead. The spearhead is long and leaf shaped with a midrib; split socket. The shaft is short with a circular cross-section and rounded terminal; the shaft is bound in thin strips of woven hide, with a small attachment loop approximately halfway down.

Wooden spoon carved from a single piece of wood. Bowl is roughly oval, with one tapered end. Back of the bowl is flat, extending to a slightly curved handle, almost at a right angle to the bowl. Outer sides of the handle, and the rim of the bowl have burnt decoration.

A pipe, with burnished black pottery bowl [.1] and long wooden stem [.2]. The bowl is conical with a everted rim, and is decorated with bands of incised cross-hatching and grooves that run around the neck of the bowl. It has a cylindrical stem, with a band of cross-hatching where the ceramic piece of the stem meets the wooden part of the stem.

Two leopard claws bound in a rectangular cover, decorated with beads in a triangular design of green, blue, red, white, yellow and metallic brown beads. Elephant hair looping under the beadwork cover.

Four quartz projectile points or arrowheads; one lozenge shaped with contracting stem; one with triangular blade and expanding stem; two with contracting stem, one with triangular blade and one with lanceolate blade.
